newsitem.title: USA: Netanyahu takes tough stand before meeting Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu takes tough stand before meeting Clinton.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took a tough stance before a crucial meeting with President Bill Clinton on Monday, signalling no change in Israel's settlements policy and declaring he would not make concessions in the face of "terrorism".

The White House said Clinton had some new ideas to offer at the meeting, which was hastily arranged after the Middle East peace process crumbled in the last few weeks. But officials cautioned against expecting any breakthrough.

Speaking to thunderous applause from a pro-Israeli American group, Netanyahu scornfully dismissed those who challenged "our right to build apartments" in Arab East Jerusalem, the latest flashpoint in the crisis.
"We're allowing contractors to build in Har Homa ... but we're also allowing contractors to build in 10 Palestinian neighbourhoods ... That is our right, that is our obligation," he said.
Violent clashes have erupted nearly every day since Israel broke ground last month on Har Homa, a 6,500-home project on a hilltop that Palestinians call Jabal Abu Ghneim and on land each side claims.

Netanyahu scoffed at Palestinian condemnation of the project. "This simple act has been described as terrorism -- the terrorism of the walk-up rentals, the terrorism of the condominiums," he said to laughter from a packed meeting room.
The United States opposes all new Israeli settlements in the disputed territory, but has muted its public criticism in hopes of finding a way to defuse tensions.

To applause, Netanyahu said: "There's been some talk about our giving something -- making a concession in return for a real crackdown by the Palestinian authority on the terrorist organisation ... And this means pure and simple surrender to terrorism. We are are being told to pay for the privilege of not being killed. We are not going to do that."
And reasserting a rejection of Arab demands on the status of Jerusalem, he said: "I want to assure you today we will never allow Jerusalem to be redivided again. Never! Never!"

It was unclear whether Netanyahu would offer Clinton a gesture to revive U.S.-backed peacemaking launched in 1993. A final deal would have to tackle the toughest issues -- Jerusalem, borders, Jewish settlers and Palestinian refugees.

White House press secretary Mike McCurry, speaking in advance of the noon (1600 GMT) White House meeting, told reporters: "I don't anticipate announcements today because this is a work in progress, and will be a work in progress."

McCurry said a senior Palestinian delegation would meet with Clinton later this week "to follow up on some of the conversations we have today, so for obvious reasons we will be very measured in what we say today."
He and other U.S. officials made clear Clinton was resisting Israeli pressure for the United States to take a more direct role in the stalled Israeli-Palestinian talks.
Middle East envoy Dennis Ross told the American Israel Public Affairs Committee only the Israelis and the Palestinians themselves could find a way forward.

"Neither the U.S. nor anyone else is going to impose a settlement," Ross said. "Obviously, we have a role to help, but we can not impose an outcome ... we can't waive a magic wand and put things back on track."

Vice President Al Gore made clear on Sunday that Clinton was not receptive to Netanyahu's public suggestion that it may take U.S.-led negotiations, like those conducted by President Jimmy Carter in 1978 at Camp David, to break the impasse.

Netanyahu has proposed that he and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat reach a final peace agreement within six months, and says the goal may require an intensive three-way summit like the one that led to accords between Egypt and Israel.

During the Camp David negotiations, Carter most often met separately with Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin and Egyptian President Anwar Sadat -- pressuring each one to move closer to the position of the other.
